newsitem.title: USA: Fed tighening less likely in 1997 - economist Sinai.
newsitem.headline: Fed tighening less likely in 1997 - economist Sinai.

text.p: A Federal Reserve monetary tightening in 1997 is less likely now, since inflation is stable, a prominent economist said.

"Fed tightening anytime in 1997 is much less likely now, since inflation in the two-percent to three-percent range is essentially price level stability," said Allen Sinai, chief global economist at Primark Decision Economics, Inc. in its 1997 outlook luncheon on Thursday.
"The Federal Reserve's task will be to keep inflation there, suggesting no quick move to lower interest rate even if the economy should fade, he said.
The slower-growth in U.S. economy and quiet inflation could lead to some increased growth and price inflationary pressures, which, however, will not be major ones, he noted.
Sinai forecast a 5-1/4 percent federal funds rate until at least the February 4-5, 1997 Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

With no change in Federal Reserve policy, a 2-1/2 to three percent running rate on inflation, and equal chances of higher as well as lower inflation going forward, the range for the 30-year treasrury bond yield is estimated at 6-1/4 to 6-3/4 percent, with 6-1/2 percent the mid-point value, he said.
Sinai said the favorable outlook for the U.S. stock market is derived particularly "from a new, lower long-term interest rate profile going forward."
"This is true whether the economy picks up or keeps languishing," he added.
For the dollar, the picture is still bright, Sinai said.
In the near- to intermediate-term, the dollar/yen remains 111 to 115, then 115 plus to 120 sometime in the first part of 1997, he projected.
"The positive U.S. dollar fundamentals still seem cyclical in nature...,so that its upward pattern will be irregular, uneven, and interrupted by corrections." Sinai said.
